itens.titulo: Carbon, Hydrogen, Neon, Oh My!: Google Gemini’s Updated Models Combine in Orchestrator
itens.texto: Google introduced two faster, less expensive Gemini 4 models and a way for its coding agent to hand work back and forth between models mid-task. What's new: On November 12, Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen , a model built to carry out coding and other agentic tasks quickly and at lower cost than Gemini 4 Carbon. On November 18, the company added Gemini 4 Neon , a model that rivals Carbon’s performance at an intermediate speed and cost. In addition, Antigravity, Google’s counterpart to OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code, gained Orchestrator, an option that allows larger models like Carbon or Neon to plan a task and have smaller models like Hydrogen carry it out. Input/output: Text, images, audio, and video in, text out (up to 1 million tokens of input and output combined; up to 64,000 output token by default Speed: Hydrogen, 173 tokens per second at its highest setting; Neon, 99 tokens per second, both according to Artificial Analysis Architecture: Adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon Price: Hydrogen $1.50/$7.50 per million input/output tokens via API; Neon $3.00/$15.00 per million input/tokens Weights/license: Proprietary Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture details, how Google adapted Hydrogen or Neon from Carbon, training data and methods How it works: Orchestrator divides each task between a planner and an executor instead of running one model for everything, according to Antigravity’s documentation . Unlike setups that split a task between different agents, Orchestrator keeps a single agent within a single context window (conversation) and switches the model behind it. First, the planner (either Carbon, Neon, or Argon) studies the code without changing anything. Then it writes a plan that spells out what the actor model should do. Hydrogen carries out the plan: It changes the code, builds and tests it, and confirms that the results match what the plan called for. Hydrogen hands control back to the planner when it runs into trouble, such as a check that fails twice or an interface that behaves differently than expected. The planner rewrites the plan according to Hydrogen's feedback, then passes the work back. Performance: Hydrogen trades some of Carbon’s capability for speed and lower cost, according to independent tests. Using Carbon as a planning model and Hydrogen as an actor inside Orchestrator nearly matches using Carbon alone, according to Google. Neon, meanwhile, outperforms Carbon on overall intelligence while costing less per task. Hydrogen set to high reasoning scored 51 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, roughly matching Gemini 4 Argon (50). Set to xhigh, Hydrogen scored 54, took 14.9 minutes, and cost $3.16 per task. Neon at xhigh scored 61, costing $6.44 per task and taking 25.8 minutes per task. Carbon set to high scored 60, took 32 minutes, and cost $5.48 per task at its introductory price. Google says that on Terminal-Bench, which tests an agent’s ability to complete tasks in a computer terminal, using Carbon and Hydrogen together in Orchestrator came close to Carbon’s success rate while finishing 19 percent faster and consuming 24 percent less of its token quota on average. Hydrogen’s lower price doesn’t always mean fewer tokens. Set to extra-high, Hydrogen generated 304 million output tokens over the Intelligence Index’s tests, compared with Carbon’s 205 million. Behind the news: Google made Gemini 4 Carbon widely available on November 10, following Argon in September. The power and cost of Gemini’s models roughly correspond with the weight of their element names: Hydrogen is light and fast, while Carbon is relatively heavier and more substantial. But the elementally heavier Neon is faster than Carbon, and Argon, now the least capable of Gemini’s “element” models, is heaviest of all. Why it matters: Pairing a cheaper model with a costlier one isn’t new. Anthropic’s Claude Code offers a related “ advisor ” option, in which a cheaper model does the work and consults a stronger one at key moments, such as before committing to a plan or when it gets stuck. OpenAI’s Codex lets developers assign different models to subagents , but it delegates work to them only when instructed. Sakana’s Fugu takes this logic one step further, using a dedicated orchestrator model that can call models from Google, OpenAI, or Anthropic at each step. All these efforts show that the best model for a coding task may turn out to be two or more models working together. We’re thinking: Google has made three very capable new models available within the last month. We can all be thankful for this rapid pace of progress.

itens.titulo: Gratitude for the AI Community: Changing Problems and Solutions in 2026 and Beyond
itens.texto: Dear friends, I look forward to seeing many of you at AI Dev in New York City on Monday Nov 30th! It is Thanksgiving here in the U.S., and I am reflecting on how grateful I am to be part of the AI community and for the incredible opportunities that lie ahead of us. Changes in AI are letting us do work at a pace and quality that was almost unimaginable a year ago. At the same time, this puts pressure on everyone to learn new skills. Despite AI’s amazing ability to solve verifiable tasks — like solve math problems such as the Riemann hypothesis — its far weaker performance on unverifiable tasks that require judgement means much work remains for people to do. I am fortunate to have many friends across Silicon Valley and beyond, whom I meet and sometimes collaborate with and who help keep me sharp at the cutting edge of AI. I know that not everyone has similar opportunities, which is why I treasure in-person events like AI Dev. AI Dev New York 2026 will focus on the AI Engineering Skills Map , which shows the most valuable skills for you to know to become skilled in AI Engineering. We have mapped every skill on the map — like building agentic systems, making systems secure and reliable, and coding agent foundations — to particular AI Dev sessions. I aim for everyone who attends to come away with meaningful new skills in AI Engineering, and also to come away with new friends so our community becomes stronger! The AI world can feel crazy some days, with rapid changes coming every week. I’m grateful for the many people in my life — professional and personal — who help me to experience life at a slower, more human pace. I hope you all have a chance to slow down and enjoy the company of friends and family over the coming holidays. Perhaps I’ll see you next week at AI Dev. And until then, Happy Thanksgiving! With gratitude, Andrew

itens.titulo: Adaptive Memory Management: Researchers at UCLA, Washington, and Northwestern release MEMCON for agents
itens.texto: Many agents save past experiences as text in an external store, and most search and update such memories using settings the agent’s developer chose by hand, such as the number of memories to retrieve or the schedule for removing them. Researchers developed a method that learns such settings per task and carries what it learns into similar tasks. What's new: Eric Hanchen, Zhi Zhang, and colleagues at the University of California Los Angeles, the University of Washington, and Northwestern University developed Memory as a Controlled Process (MEMCON). Their approach wraps around an existing memory backend and calls its existing store, retrieve, and forget functions, learning from experience. Key insight: The best way to use a memory store changes as an agent gains experience. (a) Early in a stream of tasks, the memory store holds few memories of solved tasks, so the similarities between them may be loose. Searching for memories that are similar to the task at hand may mislead a model more than it helps. Rather than ranking memories for similarity, the agent is better served by searching for memories of how it handled tasks of the same type. (b) Later, a reworded query may reveal something new. (c) As the memory store grows, it’s helpful to remove memories, because they compete for a limited number of retrieval slots. If a task ends with a signal of success or failure, the system that manages the memory can score the decisions involved. The system can sort tasks into types (say, calculating recommendations or comparing stock prices), and the average score per type can tell the system which setting works best for a particular kind of task. How it works: The authors used three harnesses (implemented in libraries including Lobster) with three models (GPT-4.1-mini, Claude Sonnet-4, and DeepSeek-V3.2) to execute tasks on the web and in simulated environments. They wrapped existing memory backends (such as G-memory ) with a small controller that kept a table of scores, one for each pairing of situation and a memory operation (such as retrieve or remove), and updated the scores after every task based on whether the agent had succeeded. Each time the agent was about to fetch from memory, the controller first extracted a compact state representation. It combined what was happening in the task, such as the kind of goal (as specified in the benchmark, like comparing stock prices) and whether the agent was repeating an action, with the state of the memory store, such as roughly how much it held (five possible bins) and whether a successful run from an earlier similar task existed. It picked an operation from the choices including searching memory, searching again with a reworded query, retrieving the successful run from a similar task, merging duplicate entries in the memory store, removing an entry, and skipping the search. It favored the one with the best score so far (the authors had hand-picked sensible default numbers for first time pairings) with an increase toward operations it had tried least often. The controller ran the chosen operation and added whatever came back to the model’s prompt. When a task ended, the controller scored how well it went (based on the outcome and how many steps the agent took to achieve it). It considered the memory choices it had made during that task and updated its table of scores. Choices made near the end, when the outcome was almost settled, resulted in the greatest increases or decreases. Choices made early got less, since later choices had room to correct them. Results: The authors compared MEMCON to other memory-management approaches using six benchmarks: three in which an agent acts step by step in a simulated environment, such as ALFWorld (household chores), PDDL (planning puzzles based on PlanBench ), and ScienceWorld (science experiments); and three in which it browses the web and uses tools to answer a single question, such as TriviaQA (trivia), WebWalkerQA (navigating websites), and GAIA (assistant tasks that call for tools and documents). MEMCON consistently achieved higher success rates while reducing token consumption. For instance: On ALFWorld, using a Lobster harness and GPT-4.1-mini, MEMCON (67.9 percent success) outperformed the strongest baseline, G-Memory (59.7 percent success). It reduced average input token consumption from 45,000 to 39,000 tokens per task, a 13 percent saving. On GAIA, using a Lobster harness and GPT-4.1-mini, MEMCON (22.4 percent accuracy), outperformed the strongest baseline, G-Memory (21.2 percent accuracy). Why it matters: An adaptive memory-management layer improves LLM agent performance by giving it the data it needs while reducing computational overhead. The savings and gains came from MEMCON learning to skip or shorten retrieval when retrieval would not help, and to fetch more or retrieve a successful run when retrieval would help, so it spent fewer tokens on irrelevant text while finding more useful memories. We’re thinking: One common way to optimize agentic behaviors is through training, another is through calls to the underlying model. This work suggests that a lightweight algorithm for adaptive memory management can be simpler and cheaper.

itens.titulo: AMD’s World Model Arrives: World Labs' Atlas gives developers 3D video and graphics generation for games, robotics, more
itens.texto: World Labs has opened Atlas , its latest world model, to the public, offering developers a self-serve API that lets them turn text prompts into 3D scenes and camera-controllable video that they can then export. What’s new: After announcing Atlas in September, World Labs released its new model to everyone on November 12. Users can build with its web tools such as Viewfinder, which takes a photo or photos and builds a scene from them, and Chisel, which builds scenes from reference images or written prompts. Atlas also comes with two smaller tools, Relight and Splats to Mesh, that (as the names suggest) relight scenes or convert them to meshes. Devs also get pay-as-you-go API access through prepaid credits, complete with a copy-and-paste prompt that lets an AI coding assistant take them through the setup. Users receive $10 of free API credits and a separate $10 for the web apps to get started. How it works: World Labs calls Atlas an “omni” world model, but under the hood it’s a multimodal autoregressive diffusion transformer pretrained from scratch to handle text, images, video, and 3D data. It links every image and depth map to a specific camera position that lets it render a scene from various viewpoints consistently. Generating a view costs $0.04 for the first frame and $0.008 for each subsequent frame at 720p (the highest resolution that the API offers). Turning views into refined splats is priced at $5. Atlas can work from a single image and render whatever lies outside the frame, or it can reconstruct a location using overlapping photos — as many as 64 in Viewfinder. As World Labs puts it, passing through “more input images gives Atlas more context: The more it sees, the less it imagines.” Developers chain together API calls to build end-to-end 3D workflows. One estimates camera positions and depth from input photos while another renders novel views or a full video from a single camera path. Then, follow-up calls convert those views into Gaussian splats and the splats into polygon meshes, complete with textures for display or simplified colliders for game engines and simulators. Performance: On Rapidata’s public leaderboard , Atlas led 19 video and world models at following camera-movement instructions, and human raters favored it in 76.7 percent of head-to-head matchups. In World Labs’ own tests of 3D reconstruction across seven datasets Atlas averaged approximately 12 percent less error than the next-best model, Pi3X, although it didn’t lead on every dataset. There isn’t much independent evidence yet; World Labs hasn’t published a model card or a paper, and no outside group has reproduced its reconstruction results. Behind the news: World Labs, co-founded by Fei-Fei Li, made its Marble world model public a year ago and later offered it to developers through an API. Atlas builds scenes in the same 3D format as Marble. World Labs’ initial Atlas announcement had a significant focus on building simulated environments to train robots. The November launch leads with web apps and 3D pipelines. Its launch page still lists robotics research and simulation as a use, but the new developer docs don’t mention robotics. In September 2026, AMD agreed to acquire World Labs in an all-stock deal valued at about $8.2 billion. The deal closed on November 16 , officially naming Li AMD’s chief scientist and executive VP. Neither AMD’s initial announcement nor its closing statement mentions Atlas or says what will happen to World Labs’ products. Why it matters: Atlas supplies 3D output that developers can use in their own projects elsewhere. Its splats and meshes can go into game engines and Blender , whereas other world models that stream pixels produce only video. Setting exact camera positions gives developers way more control than describing a camera move in a prompt. And since the onboarding is written for coding agents, a developer can ask an agent to build a scene in plain language. But there are trade-offs. Free-tier outputs can’t be used commercially, and the accuracy claims rest mostly on World Labs’ own tests. We’re thinking: Many of this fall’s most impressive world-model demos (Google DeepMind’s Genie 4, Runway’s GWM Worlds 2) were interactive videos that only a limited few can actually get their hands on. Atlas currently has a leg up on both for a pretty simple reason: it comes with a price list and an export button. Developers find out what a model is useful for by building with it. With Atlas, they can try it out for themselves.

itens.titulo: Claude Fable Gets a Price Cut: Anthropic releases Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 shortly before record-breaking IPO
itens.texto: Anthropic updated its most capable public model and removed safeguards for its private twin, opening Claude Mythos to more organizations that apply for access. Meanwhile, the company began selling shares to the public for the first time at a market capitalization of $1.5 trillion. What’s new: Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5.2 , which costs 20 percent less per token than Claude Fable 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2, a version with fewer biology and cybersecurity safeguards, is available only to organizations that Anthropic approves. Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture, training data and methods Weights/license: Proprietary Price: Via API 8/0.20/$40 per million input/cached/output tokens with cache writes at 10/16 per million tokens for five-minute/one-hour caches and 50 percent off for batched requests; fast mode 16/80 per million input/output token. Availability: Claude Fable 5.2 via Claude apps on eligible paid plans, Claude Code, Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Claude Models on Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry, with 30-day data retention required; Claude Mythos 5.2 only to organizations approved through Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program or Life Sciences Verification Program Performance: First on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index v5.0.1 (65), Vals AI’s Vals Index (71.31 percent), and ARC Prize’s ARC-AGI-3 in its standard harness (81.2 percent) Knowledge cutoff: June 2026 Features: Reasoning always on, with five reasoning levels (low, medium, high, xhigh, max), defaults to high in API and medium in Claude apps and Claude Code; tool use; fast mode, which generates tokens up to 2.5 times faster Input/output: Text and images in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens, 112 tokens per second) How it works: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are one model with different safeguards. Anthropic described one change to how it trained the model and several to how it restricts the model’s use. Another anti-distillation measure, which Anthropic calls “preserved thinking” and now applies to all API accounts rather than only new ones, stops anyone from editing earlier turns of a conversation to extract the model’s reasoning. To deter distillation (training a model on another model’s outputs), Anthropic added protections, such as showing users only a summary of the model’s reasoning. Claude models now screen requests that try to extract these traces. The company says this cuts the data distillers collect by 90 to 99 percent. In Claude Fable 5.2, classifiers block high-risk cybersecurity work such as penetration testing (simulated attacks on a system to find vulnerabilities) and generating exploits. Blocked requests route to older models: Claude Opus 4.8 answers barred cybersecurity requests, and Claude Opus 5 answers barred biology requests and a small set of requests about developing AI models. Anthropic says the cybersecurity and biology classifiers are as robust as Claude Fable 5.1’s but block about 55 percent fewer requests; the company describes these as legitimate requests blocked by mistake. During training, Anthropic limited the model’s progress in two skills that can speed development of AI models: optimizing kernels for AI chips and improving large language model architectures. Anthropic says the model performs at about the level of Claude Opus 5.5 in these areas, and that related skills such as agentic coding, hardware development, and “traditional” machine learning research were not limited. Performance: Claude Fable 5.2 ranks first on independent intelligence leaderboards from Artificial Analysis and Vals AI, but its cost per task is the highest of any model Artificial Analysis has priced. In Anthropic’s tests, Fable 5.2 improved most (relative to its predecessor) on a test of paid freelance projects. In Anthropic’s tests on the Remote Labor Index , 240 paid freelance projects in areas such as game development, architecture, and data analysis, Claude Fable 5.2 set to high reasoning produced work that human evaluators judged at least as good as the freelancers’ on 41.3 percent of projects, leading all models with more than twice the success rate of Claude Fable 5.1. On Arena AI’s Agent Arena , which ranks models by how they perform in real user sessions based on task success, user satisfaction, and steerability, Claude Fable 5.2 ranks first, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5. It also leads Agent Arena’s coding category (33.17 percent net improvement). On Arena AI’s WebDev leaderboard, which ranks models via blind head-to-head comparisons of websites they build, Claude Fable 5.2 ranks first (1,826 Elo) narrowly ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (1,816 Elo). On Vals AI’s Vals Index , which combines eight tests of finance, coding, legal, and tax work, Claude Fable 5.2 set to max reasoning ranks first (71.31 percent accuracy, $17.94 and 43.7 minutes per test), ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (70.85, $16.18 and 86 minutes per test) and Gemini 4 Carbon (70.45, $10.51 and 47.75 minutes per test). Among individual tests, it ranks first on Finance Agent v2.1, financial analysis tasks (69.47 percent); EMB v1.1, financial modeling in spreadsheets (77.38 percent); Vibe Code Bench v1.1, building apps from plain-language requests (93.77 percent); ProgramBench, rebuilding programs from scratch (19.00 percent); and BioMysteryBench, biology data investigations developed by Anthropic (83.70 percent). It ties Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 66 long tasks in a computer terminal (65.15 percent), and matches several models with a perfect score on ProofBench v1.1, formally verified math proofs. On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index v5.0.1, a weighted average of nine tests of knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge, Claude Fable 5.2 set to max reasoning ranks first (65 points, $26.54 and 40.9 minutes per task), ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon (60 points at $5.48 per task) and Claude Opus 5.5 (59 at $10.04 per task). itens.titulo: Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang steps down after scandal, succeeded by CFO Colette Kress
itens.texto: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with a possible asset for China’s intelligence agency threw the GPU giant into turmoil, leading to Huang’s apologetic resignation and the Nvidia board’s appointments of Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and Harvey Jones as its first chairman. The scandal brought renewed attention to Nvidia’s central role as a funder of and supplier to the global AI ecosystem, along with China-based companies’ access to advanced AI chips. What’s new: Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with Huang Le, who is also known as Alice Huang (the two are unrelated) as early as 2023. Ms. Huang held a high position at Megaspeed, a Singaporean company that supplies processing power to Chinese AI companies. Unusually, U.S. intelligence personnel concluded in 2025 that Ms. Huang was passing information to China, but did not provide a defensive briefing to Mr. Huang or Nvidia, which is typical practice when U.S. citizens or companies are known targets of a foreign intelligence service. After allegations that Ms. Huang was a spy were published in The New York Times , Nvidia’s board of directors announced an independent investigation into the matter. A relationship with an employee also came to light, and Mr. Huang resigned. There are no indications that Jensen Huang knew that Ms. Huang was a spy. How it works: Nvidia designs the most capable chips for training and running AI. The U.S. government restricts exports of Nvidia’s most capable products to China, but the policy has proven porous: the company’s latest chips can legally reach Southeast Asia, where data centers like Megaspeed’s serve China-based customers. Jensen Huang has opposed export restrictions throughout, arguing that their main effect is to push China to build its own chip industry. Eventually, Nvidia and the Trump administration reached a compromise: Nvidia could sell some of its H200 chips directly to China, while the U.S. would charge a 25 percent export tariff. Exports of Nvidia’s most powerful B200 and B300 GPUs would still be barred to China. But China moved to block U.S. chip imports, claiming that Nvidia GPUs could enable U.S. spying. Instead, China has pressed its own chip designers and fabricators to build domestic substitutes. Between June 2024 and February 2026, a Megaspeed affiliate in Malaysia spent $4.8 billion on Nvidia chips and other AI infrastructure, The New York Times reported . In late 2024, the U.S. Commerce Department investigated a Megaspeed site in Malaysia and found Nvidia chips still in their boxes, as though staged for shipment elsewhere. Nvidia later said it had reviewed the situation and found no evidence to support suspicions that Megaspeed was evading U.S. restrictions. Speculations about Ms. Huang's role were published in 2025. Megaspeed claimed that Ms. Huang left the company in August of that year. She is believed to have left Singapore and returned to Beijing at that time. In mid-2025, the U.S. government probed Megaspeed on suspicion that it had diverted chips to China, claims both Nvidia and Megaspeed denied. At this time, Nvidia said it stopped selling Megaspeed chips. Nvidia also stopped separately reporting GPU sales to Singapore. Also in 2025, U.S. government officials learned of Jensen Huang’s relationship with Huang Le. In spring 2026, a top-secret memo circulated among senior officials, including President Trump, asserting that China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Ms. Huang to gather information about Jensen Huang that might help Beijing evade U.S. export restrictions. Reporters at The New York Times made Jensen Huang’s relationship  with Huang Le public in late October 2026, along with the charge that Ms. Huang gathered information for Chinese intelligence. On November 11, Nvidia’s board convened an emergency meeting, then announced a CEO transition . Jensen Huang resigned and Colette Kress assumed duties as interim CEO. Less than a week later, Mr. Huang announced that he would resume CEO duties if asked. But newly appointed chair Harvey Jones said on an earnings call for investors that the board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and did not have plans to reinstate him. Yes, but: Jensen Huang’s position on selling GPUs to China was established long before his relationship with Ms. Huang. As Nvidia's CEO, his responsibility was to grow the business, including in the world’s largest market. As an American and Taiwanese citizen, he consistently argued that selling chips to mainland China was good for U.S. and Taiwanese security, since it would make China more dependent on U.S. and Taiwanese technology. Further, he shared this view with many other government and business leaders. Why it matters: Mr. Huang’s tenure tremendously benefitted the field of AI by providing critical computing technology to developers large and small. The rapid rise of AI put his company at the heart of U.S. national economics and security. Nvidia became the leading supplier of AI chips, responsible for 90 percent of all semiconductor revenue, and, for a time, the most valuable public company in the world. Nvidia under Huang was among the biggest boosters of open weight AI models, whether through its own Nemotron series, its acquisition of Hugging Face, or support for models outside its own ecosystem. Moreover, Nvidia privately funds Anthropic, OpenAI, and Safe SuperIntelligence; invests in CoreWeave, Nebius, Nokia, and xAI; and provides financial support and equipment for the world’s largest data center projects. Under interim CEO Kress (and a great deal more scrutiny from investors and regulators), Nvidia has promised to be more “disciplined” in its capital investments, signaling that its role as an AI “lender of last resort” might be gradually curtailed. We’re thinking: Three U.S. administrations have tried to keep advanced semiconductors out of China. The effort is not only ineffective, it’s counterproductive for prosperity worldwide and leads ot

itens.titulo: Jensen Huang's Legacy and Future: How Nvidia's founder saw opportunities other people couldn't
itens.texto: Dear friends, I was saddened to hear about Jensen Huang resigning from Nvidia last week. Yes, Jensen made serious mistakes . At the same time, he is a brilliant leader that has done tremendous work growing AI — providing compute to power training and inference, championing open source, and more — while turning Nvidia into one of the most valuable companies in the world. Much has been written about Jensen’s unique contributions. I still remember years ago, when I made my early push to use GPUs for training neural networks . Jensen met this idea with a positive reception, and he provided resources to help my teams at Stanford and Google and — long before it was obvious to most people that this was a good idea — directed Nvidia to shift to serving deep learning workloads. This bold call was one of many that led to Nvidia’s success. I appreciate particularly that, to ensure Nvidia’s success, he focused on building a thriving AI ecosystem that enabled many other teams to flourish. In many large companies, there is a mantra that no one is irreplaceable. In hindsight, this statement certainly did not apply to Jensen. Nvidia’s board may yet reinstate him as CEO, but if not, I wonder what future contributions he could have made to Nvidia that we will miss out on — and never know we missed. I hope everyone will see in Jensen’s critical role a refutation of the idea that people are replaceable. We should try to build teams that are robust enough to survive any individual’s departure. But at the same time, we should try to make contributions that others will look back on and understand were indispensable. Jensen is a hero of the AI world. When I wrote the blurb for his TIME 100 Award , I remember thinking there was so much more I could have written about him than would fit in the word count. I’m confident he will continue to make huge contributions. Let us all take inspiration from his example of the difference a single person can make and strive to contribute as much as we can. Keep building! Andrew

News Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with a possible asset for China’s intelligence agency threw the GPU giant into turmoil, leading to Huang’s apologetic resignation and the Nvidia board’s appointments of Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and Harvey Jones as its first chairman. The scandal brought renewed attention to Nvidia’s central role as a funder of and supplier to the global AI ecosystem, along with China-based companies’ access to advanced AI chips. What’s new: Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with Huang Le, who is also known as Alice Huang (the two are unrelated) as early as 2023. Ms. Huang held a high position at Megaspeed, a Singaporean company that supplies processing power to Chinese AI companies. Unusually, U.S. intelligence personnel concluded in 2025 that Ms. Huang was passing information to China, but did not provide a defensive briefing to Mr. Huang or Nvidia, which is typical practice when U.S. citizens or companies are known targets of a foreign intelligence service. After allegations that Ms. Huang was a spy were published in The New York Times , Nvidia’s board of directors announced an independent investigation into the matter. A relationship with an employee also came to light, and Mr. Huang resigned. There are no indications that Jensen Huang knew that Ms. Huang was a spy. How it works: Nvidia designs the most capable chips for training and running AI. The U.S. government restricts exports of Nvidia’s most capable products to China, but the policy has proven porous: the company’s latest chips can legally reach Southeast Asia, where data centers like Megaspeed’s serve China-based customers. Jensen Huang has opposed export restrictions throughout, arguing that their main effect is to push China to build its own chip industry. Eventually, Nvidia and the Trump administration reached a compromise: Nvidia could sell some of its H200 chips directly to China, while the U.S. would charge a 25 percent export tariff. Exports of Nvidia’s most powerful B200 and B300 GPUs would still be barred to China. But China moved to block U.S. chip imports, claiming that Nvidia GPUs could enable U.S. spying. Instead, China has pressed its own chip designers and fabricators to build domestic substitutes. Between June 2024 and February 2026, a Megaspeed affiliate in Malaysia spent $4.8 billion on Nvidia chips and other AI infrastructure, The New York Times reported . In late 2024, the U.S. Commerce Department investigated a Megaspeed site in Malaysia and found Nvidia chips still in their boxes, as though staged for shipment elsewhere. Nvidia later said it had reviewed the situation and found no evidence to support suspicions that Megaspeed was evading U.S. restrictions. Speculations about Ms. Huang’s role were published in 2025. Megaspeed claimed that Ms. Huang left the company in August of that year. She is believed to have left Singapore and returned to Beijing at that time. In mid-2025, the U.S. government probed Megaspeed on suspicion that it had diverted chips to China, claims both Nvidia and Megaspeed denied. At this time, Nvidia said it stopped selling Megaspeed chips. Nvidia also stopped separately reporting GPU sales to Singapore. Also in 2025, U.S. government officials learned of Jensen Huang’s relationship with Huang Le. In spring 2026, a top-secret memo circulated among senior officials, including President Trump, asserting that China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Ms. Huang to gather information about Jensen Huang that might help Beijing evade U.S. export restrictions. itens.titulo: GPT-6.2 Astra & Sol cut prices to match Claude: Alibaba updates to Qwen4; developers await open models
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: All the new models announced at Microsoft Ignite MDASH, a GitHub scanner that fixes bugs, not just reports them Nvidia’s board chair says no to reinstating Jensen Huang Nvidia halts sales of last-generation H200 GPUs to China But first: GPT-6.2 Astra leads all models in scientific work Artificial Analysis reports that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra places second on its Intelligence Index, behind only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2. Astra gained 5 points over GPT-6 Astra and now sits above Gemini 4 Carbon (60) and Claude Opus 5.5 (59) at top effort settings, while GPT-6.2 Sol gained 2 points to reach 57, matching GPT-6 Astra at about 15 percent of the cost per task. Astra is priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, 20 percent below GPT-6 Astra, with cached input cut to $0.40 from $1.00; Sol stays at $2 and $10. The models lead the site’s science, 3D and robotics evaluations, but the Coding Agent Index is flat for Astra and down 3 points for Sol, and both hallucinate often on factual questions (59 percent for Astra, 55 percent for Sol at max effort). For most software developers, the results suggest that coding-heavy workloads gain little from the upgrade, while the Sol result and the lower Astra price give cheaper options for science, knowledge and agentic work. ( Artificial Analysis ) Alibaba debuts new flagship proprietary model Alibaba released Qwen4-Max, its newest large language model, on Alibaba’s cloud platform. The model has 2.4 trillion parameters but activates only 71 billion at a time, backed by 328 billion N-gram parameters that cache frequently repeated calculations. Its training uses a residual connection (a shortcut that lets gradients skip layers) with four gated channels instead of the usual single one, and its attention mechanism adds Gated DeltaNet and QSA to cut hardware needs and skip unneeded data. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding challenges, Alibaba says Qwen4-Max beat Qwen3.8-Max while using up to 49% fewer tokens. Alibaba also open-sourced Qwen-Live-Delivery-Plugin, which has the model return a quick first draft and refine it as users give feedback, and plans to open-source smaller models built on the same techniques later. This model is proprietary, but Alibaba said it would release smaller open weight models in the Qwen4 family. ( Silicon Angle ) Microsoft debuts models for coding, images, updated Copilot Microsoft announced six AI models at its Ignite conference, covering coding, cybersecurity, image generation, transcription and real-time voice. The lead model, MAI Code 2, delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol’s performance at 40% of the price and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s at 5% of the cost, according to Microsoft. MAI Code 2 Flash is a smaller model that Microsoft says matches GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price, and MAI Cyber 2 Flash is said to beat GPT-6 Astra on a security benchmark at under 2% of the cost per task. The comparisons use selected benchmarks, some of the price gaps reflect promotional discounts, and Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman acknowledged a model tuned for everyday coding will be weaker at advanced math or science. MAI Code 2 will be available in GitHub Copilot, and enterprise customers can license model weights to customize with their own data, but only on Azure, so Copilot users may soon be running Microsoft’s own models in place of OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. ( Axios ) GitHub study focuses on AI bug fixes, not just reports GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot in which Microsoft’s Codename MDASH scanner, which uses the MAI Cyber model, looked for security bugs in six open source projects: AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick, and Netty. It flagged thousands of possible issues. A GitHub Security Lab triage agent removed duplicates and invalid findings, then seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers spent about two days per project verifying the rest by hand. That left 99 reports, sent privately through GitHub’s private vulnerability reporting, each with a suggested fix. As of November 15, maintainers had fixed 55 of them, 14 in a release; Caddy’s maintainers fixed all 22 of theirs within a week, and an ImageMagick maintainer said a report that normally takes 30 to 60 minutes to read and fix took 15. The authors note that six projects is a small sample and that the manual review does not scale yet. The pilot’s model for AI-assisted reporting is to check each finding against the project’s threat model and security policy, report it privately, and include a fix — the researchers note that AI-assisted bug reports are plentiful, but AI bug fixes remain scarce. ( GitHub ) Nvidia board not interested in bringing back Jensen Huang On Nvidia’s Q3 earnings call, new board chair Harvey Jones said the board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation and does not intend to reinstate him as CEO. Jones said the board would not take questions on the circumstances of the resignation or the ongoing investigation. Earlier the same day, Huang posted on X that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone,” and would cooperate with the board’s investigation, but offered to return as CEO if the board decided that was best for the company. Since his November 12th resignation, stories about Huang have focused on multiple reported marital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st. For developers who depend on Nvidia hardware and CUDA, the call offered no long-term successor or product guidance, so the company’s near-term direction depends on the internal investigation and the congressional testimony. itens.titulo: Gemini 4 Hydrogen balances accuracy and speed: Open source llama.cpp finally reaches version 1.0.0
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: Jensen Huang steps down, Colette Kress named interim CEO Google releases most promising decision model yet Runway’s Praxis-1 leads on robotics simulation benchmark Cloud-native developers top 21 million, strain open source But first: Google debuts a fast model to complement Carbon, replace 3.8 Flash Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster model in the Gemini 4 family than Carbon and Argon, and made it available across AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini app, Search, and Google Antigravity. Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, flat across a 1 million-token context window, with four thinking levels: low, medium, high (the default), and a new xhigh. Google says Hydrogen scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at the default level (54 at xhigh) against Argon’s 50, and finishes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash. Google also added Orchestrator to Antigravity, which switches between models such as Carbon and Hydrogen within one session; on Terminal-Bench 4.0 it reached near-Carbon success rates while using 24% less quota and finishing 19% faster, by Google’s measurement. Teams on Gemini 3.8 Flash have a cheaper, faster migration target, and Orchestrator offers a way to split planning and execution across models without managing the routing themselves. ( Google ) Llama.cpp gets first major update since 2023 The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face released v1.0.0 of both libllama and libggml, the project’s first major version after about 3.5 years of development. From now on, breaking changes to the public C API or ABI in each library’s include directory will trigger a major-version bump, while backward-compatible features, backend updates, and model support get minor bumps and bug fixes get patches. The project now ships through Docker, Debian, Homebrew, conda-forge, MacPorts, Winget, and an XCFramework for iOS and macOS, plus pre-release artifacts for Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, and iOS. It supports more than 150 model architecture variants and the mainstream speculative decoding methods, and runs CI on self-hosted runners with hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM, and Intel. Developers who link against libllama or libggml can now treat the version number as a signal for when an upgrade will break their build, and can pin to a major version in package managers. ( Hugging Face ) Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang resigns Following his admission of an extramarital affair and a rapid third-party investigation, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO, and board member, effective immediately, after 33 years at the company. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO while keeping her CFO role, and the board has begun a search that will consider internal and external candidates. Harvey C. Jones, a former Synopsys CEO, was appointed the board’s first-ever chair. The company says operations, customer commitments, and the product roadmap will continue without interruption, and the third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings report stays scheduled for November 17. ( Nvidia ) Google releases decision model that rivals Jev at higher price Google released the Gemini Decisions API, backed by a new model, gemini-decision-1, that returns calibrated probabilities for typed questions instead of generating text. One request takes a shared input (text, image, audio, video, or PDF) and up to 1,000 questions, each a yes/no, a choice among 2 to 255 options, or a score on a rubric of up to 255 levels. Input costs $0.10 per 1M tokens, output tokens are always zero, and the shared input is billed once per request; Google reports 150-250 ms end-to-end latency for inputs up to 16K tokens. In Google’s self-reported benchmarks, the model leads 7 of 9 accuracy tests and has a top-1 calibration error of 0.0250, about half the 0.0494 of TypeSafe Jev1.14, but it trails Jev 1.14 on When2Call (79.9% vs 82.0%) and Mind2Web Multimodal (86.2% vs 86.8%) and costs more per token ($0.10 vs $0.042). It runs only on Google’s hosted API, with a 262,144-token context and no prompt caching or Batch API. For agent builders, this replaces generate-then-parse for routing, policy checks and grading with numeric outputs they can branch on. Note that the benchmark figures are unverified and repeated context is billed in full on every call. ( MarkTechPost ) Runway publishes open-weight robotics model Runway released Praxis-1, a robot control model, with open weights and source code under the commercial-use-friendly Apache 2.0 license. The model takes camera images, text instructions, and the robot’s position data, predicts how the scene will change, and outputs matching robot movements. It builds on a video model fine-tuned with human-action videos and robot data, and it still needs adaptation per robot: about 277 hours of DROID data for a Franka arm, and 1,400 to 2,600 hours for a dual-arm robot. On Nvidia’s RoboLab-120 simulation leaderboard Runway reports a 46.2 percent success rate, ahead of FLUX 3 Action at 42.9 percent among World Action Models. Note that Runway ran the tests itself and they are not independently verified. For developers, the weights and code are on Hugging Face and GitHub. However, the standard model needs an 80 GB GPU; the compressed version is estimated to fit a 32 GB RTX 5090 without a measured memory figure. ( The Decoder ) Cloud-native developers grow by millions, lead AI adoption The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and research firm SlashData’s latest State of Cloud Native Development report counts more than 21 million cloud-native developers, or 41% of developers worldwide. About 75% of them use AI in some form, compared with about 55% of other developers, according to SlashData’s Liam Bollmann-Dodd. CNCF’s Bob Killen said the headcount likely undercounts, since many people consume cloud-native applications without knowing it.

itens.titulo: Retrieval for RAG-Resistant Docs: An agent that searches, outlines, and reads entire documents outperforms chunk-and-embed retrieval
itens.texto: Retrieving documents chunk by chunk works well with many types of text, but it can fail with documents in which the meaning of a given span — say, numbers in a table — depends on particulars found elsewhere on the page — say, the label of their units. Researchers assigned agents to keep all the necessary information in view. What’s new: Sagar Tamang, Ayush Vyas, and Tabarakul Hazarika at Indian Institute of Technology Patna and TwoSpoon, an independent tech lab, developed Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search (READ). Their method replaces vector-based retrieval with an agentic harness and specialized search tools. Key insight: For RAG-style retrieval, a document is divided into chunks that are embedded, and a model retrieves chunks whose embeddings are similar to the embedding of the query. But this approach can fail with documents such as financial or scientific reports, where numbers in a table gain important meaning from units or dates that may lie many lines away, or legal briefs, in which words may have special meanings that are defined many paragraphs away. An agent with tools to navigate undivided documents can look beyond predefined chunks. How it works: The authors used the READ method with Gemini 2.5 Pro. The system had access to three tools: (i) A keyword-search tool returned matching line numbers, (ii) an outline tool listed section headings with line numbers, and (iii) a text-reader tool fetched specific line ranges. Given a query like, “What is the mathematical difference between the Fiscal Deficit and the Revenue Surplus for the year 2024-2025?,” the READ agent activated a loop that generated a search term such as “Fiscal Deficit,” scanned a document for the term, checked matching line(s) against the document outline, and read the text from the table headers to the matching line(s). Within the loop, the model refined its query when it got too many hits, too few hits, or insufficient information to make sense of what it found. Each refinement repeated the loop with a new search term or a new range to be read. Results: The authors used READ, RAG-style retrieval, and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop to answer 51 questions about a 780-page financial report published by the government of Gujarat, India. All systems were based on Gemini 2.5 Pro. READ answered 58.8 percent of the questions correctly, outperforming both RAG-style retrieval (15.7 percent) and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop (27.5 percent) Why it matters: Chunk-and-embed retrieval methods tend not to work well with documents in which the meaning of any given passage is not self-contained, such as financial reports, contracts, and regulatory filings. In such cases, letting a model search the whole document is more effective. We’re thinking: Chunk-and-embed has its place, but letting agents write search queries can be a better approach. Beyond READ and RLM (covered in last week’s issue of The Batch ), Search-R1 trains LLMs to reason their way through multi-turn searches, and IRCoT uses an LLM’s reasoning traces as a search query.

itens.titulo: Search Engine Wars, AI Edition: Google makes less money on LLM-powered search even as OpenAI works to attract its users
itens.texto: Google is turning its search engine into a chatbot, and OpenAI is turning its chatbot into a search engine. Yet neither company has made AI-powered search bring in as much revenue per query as traditional search links. What’s new: On October 29, the day after Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported its financial statement for July through September, its market value fell by nearly $500 billion, its biggest one-day decline on record, The Wall Street Journal reported . Google’s search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent, down from 19 percent and 17 percent in the previous two quarters. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s business expanded, presumably including many queries that once would have been entered into a search engine. An OpenAI executive said ChatGPT’s weekly users had grown from 1 billion to 1.2 billion in two months, and it claims to handle roughly one-fifth as many searches as Google. How Google search pays: Google makes money when advertisers pay for their messages to appear beside search results, but that business is shrinking. Google collected $63.35 billion from traditional search and related ads from July through September, including ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode. The number of queries it received grew at its fastest rate in five years Google didn’t reveal how much of that revenue came from AI Mode, but an AI Mode query brings in less revenue than a comparable traditional search, because it shows fewer ads and advertisers pay less for them, Ars Technica wrote . In effect, Google’s AI is cannibalizing its search business. How AI search ads work: Meanwhile, both Google and OpenAI are pushing ads into AI-generated search results. On the day it issued its financial report, Google said AI Mode will show ads in 11 countries , up from 1 previously. In the U.S., ads will appear when a user enters a follow-up query. OpenAI, which began to test ads early this year, now shows them in 89 countries to users of ChatGPT's free and low-cost Go plans. OpenAI says its ad sales reached a pace of $1 billion per year within 200 days of launch, a figure that hasn't been verified independently. That works out to about $250 million every three months, compared with Google's $63.35 billion. Yes, but: OpenAI is a private company, so it's impossible to assess how much of Google's search business ChatGPT actually has taken, and estimates vary widely. When it said it processed one-fifth the number of searches Google does, it didn’t explain which Google figure it compared against, Search Engine Journal noted . In February, the search-marketing firm Ahrefs estimated 12 percent, using a different definition of search. Behind the news: While Google and OpenAI compete for AI-powered search, the web publishers whose pages AI models use to generate search results are seeking more control over how AI companies use their work. One proposal would let them put a flag on their pages that would ask AI developers not to use them to train models. Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic said they plan to honor the flag. Meanwhile, Google offers publishers a way to exempt their pages from AI Overviews and AI Mode. Why it matters: AI has many uses, but it’s not yet entirely clear how to build highly profitable businesses on it. AI-powered search could be one answer, since advertisers already pay to reach users through search engines. Ironically, AI is drawing more people to search faster than it’s drawing advertising money. But until AI search ads earn as much as the traditional ads they replace, relying purely on AI search for revenue doesn’t seem like a surefire way to replicate Google’s previous success. We’re thinking: Chatbots may eventually eat into users’ web searches, but the users of the future won’t necessarily be people. AI agents carrying out tasks such as shopping on a user's behalf will also see ads that could sway their behavior or recommendations to users. In fact, Time magazine already sells ads aimed at agents instead of people .

itens.titulo: LLMs Can Fine-Tune Neural Networks: Researchers used GPT-6 Astra to improve a small model’s performance by editing its weights
itens.texto: Research suggests that you can improve a neural network’s weights simply by prompting an LLM — for networks of less than 1 billion parameters, at least. What’s new: Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, and colleagues from MIT showed that GPT-6 Astra can interpret, improve, and produce neural network weights in proof-of-concept studies . How it works: The authors asked GPT-6 Astra to (a) identify which game a network was trained on based on its weights, (b) alter the weights of a network to improve its ability to operate a simulated car, and (c) generate a network that would win a game. In a more practical experiment, they asked GPT-6 Astra to improve Qwen3.5-0.8B’s math performance. The authors trained four tiny vanilla neural networks (17,000 parameters each) separately to play Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Frogger. Given the weights and asked “Which game was this neural network trained on?” GPT-6 Astra was able to identify the game in all four cases. The authors trained a vanilla neural network (171,000 parameters) to drive a car up a ramp in the Kinetix environment but suspended the training when the car failed to climb the ramp. They fed GPT-6 Astra a description of the problem, the goal, the model weights, and one of the actions the model took during a failed run. GPT-6 Astra edited 3.5 percent of the vanilla neural network’s weights, enabling it to succeed in all 1,024 attempts. They gave GPT-6 Astra the rules and source code of a game (specifically Breakout, Seaquest, or Asterix) and a 20,000-parameter network whose weights were initialized to 0, and asked it to generate a model that would play the game. They trained networks of the same size and type for comparison. The generated models achieved higher scores than the manually trained ones at 100 million training steps. However, the trained models were more competitive at 500 million training steps: Of the three games, Astra led on one, roughly tied on one, and lost on the third. GPT-6 Astra, given Qwen3.5-0.8B’s weights, a tool to run it, and the training set for the MATH-500 and GSM8K math benchmarks, was asked to improve its benchmark performance. It found that Qwen3.5-0.8B often looped, filling its context window unnecessarily, and modified 0.016 percent of the weights. The change boosted performance on MATH-500 from 7.9 percent to 48.1 percent. Yes, but: Not all case studies yielded positive results. Asking GPT-6 Astra to improve Gemma 3 270M’s math performance did not work. GPT-6 Astra didn’t find any looping or other obvious issue, and so it was unable to improve the Gemma 3 270M’s performance. Why it matters: These results are proofs of concept that have not been shown to extend to more diverse LLMs and target models. However, they show how LLMs could be used in building models. They might improve interpretability, enabling us to better understand the networks we build. Or they might facilitate network editing or generation, making it possible to diagnose and fix obvious issues or accelerate training. We're thinking: If neural network editing holds true at larger scales, this holds massive promise: It’s much cheaper to run a network once than to fine-tune one.

itens.titulo: GPT-6 Cyber Patches More Security Flaws for Less Cost: OpenAI’s security-tuned version of GPT-6 Astra closed root-level Linux holes for $1,280 each
itens.texto: OpenAI built a cybersecurity model that discovered, exploited, and patched nearly 950 severe vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel in a single run. What’s new: GPT-6 Cyber , a version of GPT-6 Astra fine-tuned to find software vulnerabilities, is restricted initially to approved customers. In a mid-October scan of the Linux kernel, GPT-6 Cyber generated working exploits for 948 flaws that allow ordinary users to gain full control of a machine. The run cost $1,213,430 in API calls, around $1,279 per exploit. (In July, the same harness running GPT-5.6 Sol exploited 166 such vulnerabilities for a total cost of $513,690, around $3,095 per exploit.) Input/output: Text and images in (up to 1,050,000 tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens) Features: Reasoning, tool use, streaming, structured outputs Performance: More capable than GPT-6 Astra on most tests of cybersecurity conducted by OpenAI Availability: Initially offered to selected customers of OpenAI’s Daybreak Red advanced security program; customers must use single sign-on, multifactor authentication, managed devices, and least-privileged access and restrict API requests to specific IP addresses Price: API $20/$2/$100 per million input/cached/output tokens; cache storage $25 per million tokens for 30 minutes, $50 per million tokens for 12 hours License: Proprietary Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture, training data, training details, knowledge cutoff, reasoning levels, schedule for wider availability How it works: OpenAI fine-tuned GPT-6 Cyber via reinforcement learning on tasks such as reproducing crashes, generating working exploits, and finding code vulnerabilities. The reward function discouraged refusal of authorized security requests and reward hacking, and it encouraged the model to stay within authorized behaviors and to report results accurately. A team of agents ran a pipeline that enabled the model to find, confirm, and exploit flaws in the Linux kernel and patch them. In the pipeline, scout agents identified security-relevant parts of the kernel that ordinary users can reach. Analyst agents read the scout agents’ candidate code and flagged 2,308 flaws within 12 hours. For each candidate, a triage agent wrote a short program to trigger the flaw in a virtual machine that detected memory errors. The triage agent iterated until the flaw appeared or the agent ran out of approaches. This step confirmed 1,724 flaws within 30 hours. A screening agent reviewed the confirmed flaws and kept those that had a plausible path to root access that would confer full control of a machine. Exploit-writing agents tried to gain root access in virtual machines configured with a standard Linux distribution’s protections and produced 1,169 working exploits. The pipeline wrote patches and checked nearby code for variants of each flaw. Security researchers reviewed the exploits and proposed severity ratings before reporting them to Linux maintainers. Performance: GPT-6 Cyber proved substantially more capable than GPT-5.6 Cyber in tests by OpenAI, and it outperformed GPT-6 Astra on most benchmarks. Independent tests have not yet been published. On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT-6 Cyber set to the highest reasoning level tested (48.45 percent) outperformed GPT-6 Astra set to its highest level (42.43 percent) and GPT-5.6 Cyber (32.1 percent). On a version of ExploitGym with stronger defenses, GPT-6 Cyber (36.94 percent) outperformed GPT-6 Astra (29.69 percent). Gemini 4 Carbon, evaluated by Google without guardrails at an undisclosed reasoning level, achieved 54.8 percent. ExploitGym Honeypot instructs a model to exploit a specific target but includes an easy-to-exploit supporting service that the model may use but isn’t authorized to attack. GPT-6 Cyber attacked that service in 0.07 percent of attempts without OpenAI’s safety deployment instructions, compared with 5.51 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber and 0 percent for GPT-6 Astra. With the instructions, GPT-6 Cyber did not attack the honeypot. On FrontierCyber, 288 real-world challenges, GPT-6 Cyber solved 90 and GPT-6 Astra solved 96. Neither model solved any of the 15 hardest challenges, nor did they successfully attack a fully hardened target. Behind the news: The cybersecurity capabilities of recent top-performing AI models — which are available either in guardrailed versions or to selected customers — have set security personnel on high alert. In October, the U.S. government reported critical flaws in the PHP server coding language after OpenAI had led a coalition that addressed them in preceding months. Hackers stole $6.3 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, the biggest known crypto heist, by exploiting compromised internal AI tools. Why it matters: The latest cybersecurity models pose both challenges and opportunities for security. On one hand, they’re extremely adept at exploiting flaws. On the other, they make flaws easy and inexpensive to find and fix. Hacking competitions like Pwn2Own have offered $20,000 to $70,000 per Linux kernel exploit, yet OpenAI spent $1,279 per exploit. We’re thinking: It’s encouraging that GPT-6 Cyber without safety instructions exploited the off-limits service in only 0.07 percent of attempts in OpenAI’s honeypot test, and with safety instructions never tried. We’d like to see OpenAI help independent testers to repeat this test or others like it.
